content: We're hitting Postgres connection limits during peak traffic. Currently at max_connections=200 and our 12 service replicas are each configured with a pool of 20 connections. The math doesn't work — 12 * 20 = 240 > 200.

That's the root cause. You're oversubscribing the database connection limit. Two approaches: increase max_connections (has memory implications) or use PgBouncer as a connection pooler between your services and Postgres.

PgBouncer is the right call — I don't want to keep bumping max_connections every time we scale. The thing is, we use prepared statements heavily and I've heard PgBouncer in transaction mode doesn't support them.
That's correct for older PgBouncer versions, but PgBouncer 1.21+ supports prepared statements in transaction pooling mode. Make sure you're on a recent version.

Good to know. I'll set it up with transaction pooling — each service gets a logical pool of 20 but PgBouncer multiplexes onto a smaller set of actual connections. Fundamentally this is the same pattern as our HTTP connection pooling, just at the database layer.

Exactly. PgBouncer acts as a connection concentrator. You could set it to maintain 100 server connections to Postgres and let all 12 services share that pool. Most of the time connections are idle between query executions anyway.

Yeah, and with transaction pooling the connection is only held during the transaction, not the entire session. Our transactions are short — sub-millisecond for most reads. I'll deploy PgBouncer as a sidecar in the pod.
